title: Line Integral
body:
Integrating along a path instead of along an interval. Two kinds, and they answer different
questions, so the first job on any problem is deciding which one is being asked for.

## Scalar: $\int_C f\,ds$

$$
\int_C f\,ds = \int_a^b f(\mathbf{r}(t))\,\|\mathbf{r}'(t)\|\,dt
$$

**This is [[Arc Length]] with a weight on it**, and it is literally the same $ds$: take $f = 1$ and
you get the length of the curve back. Use it for the mass of a wire with variable density, or the
average value of a function along a path. It does not care which way you traverse $C$.

## Vector: $\int_C \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r}$

$$
\int_C \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r} = \int_a^b \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot \mathbf{r}'(t)\,dt
$$

The [[Dot Product]] keeps only the component of $\mathbf{F}$ **along** the direction of travel, so
this measures **work** done by a force along the path, or **circulation** of a flow around it. It
flips sign when the orientation flips.

| | $\int_C f\,ds$ | $\int_C \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r}$ |
|---|---|---|
| Integrand | scalar field | [[Vector Field]] |
| Element | $ds$, a length | $d\mathbf{r}$, a displacement |
| Orientation | irrelevant | **flips the sign** |
| Measures | mass, average value | work, circulation |

## Method

1. [[Parameterization|Parameterise]] $C$ as $\mathbf{r}(t)$, $a \le t \le b$, in the direction asked for
2. Substitute so the integrand is a function of $t$ alone
3. Replace $ds$ with $\|\mathbf{r}'(t)\|\,dt$ or $d\mathbf{r}$ with $\mathbf{r}'(t)\,dt$
4. Integrate over $t$ with the techniques from [[Integration Techniques]]

Step 2 is where the marks are: **substitute the parameterisation into $\mathbf{F}$ as well**, not
just into the element. Half of all errors here are a leftover $x$ or $y$.

## Two ways to avoid the work

- If $\mathbf{F}$ is a [[Conservative Vector Field]], the integral is path independent and equals
  $f(\text{end}) - f(\text{start})$ for the potential $f$. No parameterisation at all
- If $C$ is a **closed** curve in the plane, [[Green's Theorem]] converts the circulation to a
  [[Double Integral]] over the region inside, which is usually easier

Checking for those two before parameterising is the single best habit in this block.

## Related

- [[Parameterization]]: step 1, and where $ds$ and $d\mathbf{r}$ come from
- [[Arc Length]] in [[CALCULUS 2]]: the $f = 1$ case, same $ds$
- [[Conservative Vector Field]] and [[Green's Theorem]]: the two shortcuts
- [[Surface Integral]]: the same construction one dimension up
- [[Stokes' Theorem]]: relates this to the curl through a surface
- [[Vector Calculus]], [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]]
- [[Complex Integration]] in [[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]] is this same construction with a
  complex integrand. Cauchy's theorem plays the part [[Green's Theorem]] plays here, and an
  analytic function behaves exactly like a [[Conservative Vector Field]]: every closed loop
  integrates to zero
